clinical_note: A 5-month-old boy is evaluated for worsening hypotonia and poor head control that began in early infancy. His parents report prolonged feeds, weak cry, and increasing fatigue with bottle feeding over the last six weeks. Examination shows generalized muscle weakness, mild macroglossia, and reduced antigravity movements without focal neurologic deficits. Echocardiogram demonstrates hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and serum creatine kinase is elevated. There is no history of seizures, fever, or perinatal hypoxic injury. Newborn hearing screen was normal, and family history is negative for neuromuscular disease. The clinical course is progressive rather than episodic.
true_disease: Glycogen storage disease due to acid maltase deficiency

clinical_note: A 16-year-old girl is referred after a school physical noted marked tall stature and asymmetric chest wall prominence. She reports gradual worsening of nearsightedness and intermittent palpitations but denies syncope or exertional chest pain. Ophthalmology documented lens subluxation, and echocardiography shows dilation of the aortic root. Her arm span exceeds height, and exam shows arachnodactyly, pes planus, and mild scoliosis. There is no developmental delay, seizure history, or inflammatory joint swelling. Her father had surgery for an aortic aneurysm in his thirties. Symptoms have evolved slowly over adolescence.

A 15-month-old boy presents with developmental delay, recurrent otitis media, and progressive abdominal distention. Parents note that his facial features have become coarser over the last several months, and he is no longer gaining motor milestones. Examination shows macroglossia, hepatosplenomegaly, joint stiffness, and a broad nasal bridge. He has noisy breathing during sleep but no seizures or episodes of hypoglycemia. Ophthalmology found early corneal clouding, and audiology suggests conductive hearing loss. The family reports no consanguinity. The clinical picture is one of progressive multisystem storage disease.

A 6-year-old boy is seen for repeated long-bone fractures after low-impact falls since toddlerhood. His parents report that he bruises easily but has no bleeding gums, fevers, or weight loss. Physical examination shows blue-gray sclerae, mild short stature, joint laxity, and dental enamel abnormalities. Hearing is currently normal, although his mother required hearing aids as a young adult. Radiographs show osteopenia and evidence of prior healed fractures. Development and cognition are age appropriate. The pattern is chronic and skeletal rather than inflammatory or malignant.

A newborn with atypical genital appearance develops vomiting, lethargy, and poor feeding on day eight of life. Basic metabolic panel shows hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and dehydration despite adequate intake. The infant was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and has no fever or evidence of sepsis. Examination shows hyperpigmentation and ambiguous genitalia. There is no congenital heart disease, seizure activity, or structural renal anomaly. Cortisol is low with markedly elevated adrenal precursors. Symptoms improve after stress-dose steroids and mineralocorticoid replacement.

A 4-year-old boy is evaluated for delayed walking, frequent falls, and difficulty rising from the floor. His parents describe progressive trouble climbing stairs over the past year. Examination shows calf enlargement, waddling gait, proximal weakness, and a positive Gowers maneuver. Creatine kinase is markedly elevated, and there is no sensory loss or cerebellar ataxia. He has mild speech delay but no seizures or vision complaints. Family history includes a maternal uncle who used a wheelchair as a teenager. The pattern suggests progressive childhood muscular dystrophy.

A 42-year-old man is brought for evaluation of involuntary movements and personality change. His spouse reports three years of progressive irritability, impulsive spending, and worsening work performance. Neurologic examination shows choreiform movements, impaired saccades, and mild gait disturbance. He has no fever, no exposure to dopamine-blocking medications, and no history of stroke. His father developed a similar movement disorder in midlife. Cognitive screening shows reduced executive function. Symptoms have progressed gradually rather than occurring in attacks.

A 9-month-old girl is assessed for developmental regression after previously rolling and babbling appropriately. Parents report exaggerated startle to sound, loss of social engagement, and worsening truncal control. Examination shows hypotonia with emerging spasticity and a cherry-red spot on retinal exam. Head circumference has remained near the tenth percentile without hydrocephalus. There is no hepatosplenomegaly, no recurrent infections, and no known toxin exposure. Brain MRI is nonspecific. The history suggests progressive neurodegeneration beginning in infancy.

A 7-year-old boy is referred for multiple tan macules noted since infancy and new bumps on the trunk. His teacher reports attention problems, but his academic skills are only mildly delayed. Exam shows more than six cafe-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, and several soft cutaneous nodules. Ophthalmology finds Lisch nodules without optic pathway symptoms. There is no hearing loss, vestibular complaint, or family history of bilateral acoustic tumors. Blood pressure is normal. The cutaneous findings have increased gradually over childhood.

A term male newborn is admitted for persistent hypoglycemia requiring high glucose infusion. Birth weight was above the 97th percentile, and exam shows macroglossia with an umbilical wall defect repaired shortly after delivery. The infant has asymmetric overgrowth of the right leg and ear creases. There are no seizures after glucose correction, and cardiac exam is normal. Abdominal ultrasound shows enlarged kidneys without hydronephrosis. Family history is negative, and pregnancy was notable only for polyhydramnios. The neonatal overgrowth pattern raises concern for an imprinting disorder.

A 6-year-old girl is evaluated for progressive unsteady gait and slurred speech. Her parents report frequent sinus infections and prolonged cough after viral illnesses. Examination shows truncal ataxia, oculomotor apraxia, dysarthria, and small telangiectasias over the conjunctivae. She has no muscle weakness, no sensory level, and no episodes suggesting stroke. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is elevated, and immunoglobulin levels are low. Brain MRI shows cerebellar volume loss. The neurologic and immune features have worsened slowly since early childhood.

A 22-year-old man presents with gradual night vision difficulty that began in adolescence. He reports bumping into objects in dim rooms and narrowing peripheral vision over several years. Fundus examination shows bone-spicule retinal pigmentation and attenuated vessels, and electroretinogram is abnormal. There is no diabetes, optic neuritis, or history of prematurity. Hearing is normal, and neurologic examination is otherwise unremarkable. His sister has similar night blindness. The progression is retinal and degenerative rather than inflammatory.
hpo_terms: Bone spicule pigmentation of the retina
selected_symptoms: Bone spicule pigmentation of the retina

clinical_note: A 19-year-old woman is evaluated for tremor, mood changes, and abnormal liver tests. She has had worsening handwriting, intermittent dysarthria, and new depression over the past year. Examination shows mild dystonia, dysarthria, and Kayser-Fleischer rings. She denies alcohol use, acetaminophen overdose, or viral hepatitis risk factors. Laboratory testing shows low ceruloplasmin and elevated urinary copper. There is no family history of Huntington disease or early stroke. The combination of hepatic and movement findings is progressive.

A 28-year-old man reports burning pain in his hands and feet since childhood, worse with fever and exercise. He has decreased sweating, clusters of dark red skin lesions over the groin, and mild proteinuria on screening urinalysis. Ophthalmology notes corneal whorling without visual loss. There is no diabetes, alcohol misuse, or vitamin deficiency. His maternal uncle required dialysis in his forties. Echocardiogram shows early left ventricular hypertrophy. The symptoms span neuropathic, renal, dermatologic, and cardiac systems.

A 10-year-old girl is seen for chronic fatigue, easy bruising, and abdominal fullness. Examination shows splenomegaly and mild hepatomegaly without jaundice. Laboratory studies reveal thrombocytopenia and anemia, and radiographs show Erlenmeyer flask deformity with bone pain. She has no recurrent severe infections, no neurologic regression, and no inflammatory arthritis. Family ancestry is Ashkenazi Jewish. Symptoms have developed gradually over several years. Enzyme testing is ordered because a lysosomal storage disorder is suspected.

A 3-year-old boy is evaluated for developmental delay and a musty odor noticed by his parents. He has fair skin compared with siblings, eczema, and behavioral irritability. Newborn screening records are unavailable because he was born outside the country. There is no history of neonatal hypoglycemia, congenital heart disease, or recurrent infections. Examination shows microcephaly and mild growth delay. Plasma amino acids show markedly elevated phenylalanine. Dietary treatment is discussed with the family.

A 9-year-old boy has chronic productive cough, recurrent lower respiratory infections, and poor weight gain. Parents describe greasy stools and abdominal bloating since infancy. Sweat chloride is elevated on two occasions. There is no congenital heart disease, primary ciliary dyskinesia history, or immune deficiency on basic testing. Chest CT shows bronchiectasis and mucus plugging. He also has chronic sinus congestion. The pulmonary and pancreatic features have been persistent rather than episodic.

A 20-month-old girl is brought for loss of purposeful hand use and language regression. She had apparently typical early development until around 12 months, then stopped using words and developed repetitive hand-wringing movements. Parents note episodes of abnormal breathing while awake and increasing gait instability. There is no history of perinatal injury, meningitis, or progressive organ enlargement. Examination shows acquired microcephaly, dystonia, and limited eye contact. EEG is abnormal but no confirmed clinical seizures have occurred. The developmental course is regressive and stereotyped.

A 9-year-old boy is evaluated for obesity and persistent hyperphagia. He had severe neonatal hypotonia and feeding difficulty requiring a nasogastric tube, followed by rapid weight gain in early childhood. Exam shows small hands, short stature, hypogonadism, and mild intellectual disability. Sleep study shows obstructive sleep apnea. There is no retinal dystrophy, polydactyly, or renal anomaly. Parents report food-seeking behavior and temper outbursts. Endocrine testing shows growth hormone deficiency.

A 4-year-old girl presents with severe speech delay, frequent laughter, and an unusually happy affect. Parents report delayed walking, broad-based gait, and intermittent tremulous movements. She has had two generalized seizures during febrile illnesses. Examination shows microcephaly, ataxia, and hand-flapping behavior. There is no hepatosplenomegaly, no regression after normal early milestones, and no progressive weakness. EEG shows a pattern concerning for a neurogenetic syndrome. Sleep is fragmented but appetite is normal.

An 8-year-old boy is referred for academic struggles, friendly overfamiliar behavior, and a heart murmur. He has a history of infant feeding difficulty, mild hypercalcemia, and poor growth. Examination shows a broad forehead, periorbital fullness, full cheeks, and a wide mouth. Echocardiogram demonstrates supravalvular aortic stenosis, while renal ultrasound shows mild nephrocalcinosis. He has no seizures, no retinal degeneration, and no major motor regression. Parents mention sensitivity to loud sounds and anxiety at school. The phenotype suggests a contiguous gene deletion syndrome.

A 2-year-old boy is evaluated for short stature, feeding difficulty, and a newly detected cardiac murmur. He had prolonged neonatal feeding problems and delayed motor milestones but no regression. Examination shows hypertelorism, low posterior hairline, pectus deformity, and mild joint hypermobility. Echocardiogram reveals pulmonary valve stenosis. There is easy bruising but no thrombocytopenia-related bleeding crisis. He has no lens dislocation, no aortic root aneurysm, and no cafe-au-lait pattern typical of neurofibromatosis. Genetic testing is pursued for a RASopathy.

A 7-year-old boy presents after two focal seizures and worsening school performance. Parents report pale skin patches present since infancy and several small facial papules that have become more noticeable. Brain MRI shows cortical tubers and subependymal nodules. Renal ultrasound shows small angiomyolipomas but normal renal function. He has no cafe-au-lait macules, no optic glioma, and no progressive chorea. Developmental history includes autism spectrum features and attention difficulty. The findings involve skin, brain, and kidney.

A 12-year-old girl is assessed for clumsiness, vertical gaze difficulty, and declining school performance. She had neonatal jaundice and mild hepatosplenomegaly that improved, but over the last two years has developed dysphagia and gait instability. Neurologic examination shows vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and mild dystonia. There is no Kayser-Fleischer ring, and copper studies are normal. She has occasional gelastic cataplexy-like episodes but no generalized seizures. Brain MRI does not show a focal lesion. The history suggests a progressive lipid trafficking disorder.

A 4-year-old boy has coarse facial features, noisy breathing, and progressive joint stiffness. His mother reports recurrent ear infections and gradual enlargement of the abdomen. Examination shows macrocephaly, macroglossia, limited shoulder and elbow mobility, hepatosplenomegaly, and an umbilical hernia. Corneas are clear, and there is no severe early neurodevelopmental regression. Hearing evaluation shows mixed hearing loss. The patient is male, and an older maternal male relative had a similar condition. The clinical pattern suggests an X-linked mucopolysaccharidosis.

A 3-month-old girl is brought for poor head control, weak cry, and feeding fatigue. Parents note tongue twitching and reduced spontaneous leg movements. Examination shows profound hypotonia, tongue fasciculations, areflexia, and paradoxical breathing. There is no cardiomyopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, and no facial weakness suggesting congenital myopathy. Creatine kinase is normal. She has had one aspiration pneumonia after a choking episode. The course is progressive motor neuron weakness beginning in infancy.

A 14-year-old boy is evaluated for progressive gait imbalance and frequent falls. Symptoms began around age ten and have slowly worsened, with slurred speech and difficulty with fine motor tasks. Examination shows lower-limb areflexia, dysarthria, pes cavus, and impaired vibration sense. ECG shows repolarization abnormalities, and echocardiogram suggests early hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. There are no seizures, no episodic migraine, and no liver disease. His sister has similar gait problems. The picture is a progressive hereditary ataxia with neuropathy.

A 9-year-old boy is seen for self-injurious biting of the lips and fingers, developmental delay, and abnormal movements. Parents report orange crystals in the diaper during infancy and recurrent kidney stones. Examination shows spasticity, dystonic posturing, and mild intellectual disability. Uric acid is markedly elevated. There is no hepatosplenomegaly, no cherry-red spot, and no regression after normal early development. Behavioral outbursts have become harder to manage over the last year. The neurologic and metabolic findings point to purine salvage dysfunction.

A 13-year-old boy is evaluated for persistent microscopic hematuria found during a sports physical. He has mild proteinuria and a family history of male relatives with kidney failure before age forty. Audiology shows bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Eye exam notes anterior lenticonus. He has no edema, rash, arthritis, or recurrent urinary tract infections. Renal ultrasound is structurally normal. Kidney biopsy shows glomerular basement membrane abnormalities. The pattern suggests inherited basement membrane disease.

A 10-year-old girl has progressive night blindness, obesity, and learning difficulties. Parents also report extra digits removed in infancy and delayed toilet training. Examination shows truncal obesity, retinal dystrophy, mild developmental delay, and hypogonadism. Renal ultrasound shows structural urinary tract abnormalities. There is no hyperphagia beginning after neonatal hypotonia, and methylation testing for Prader-Willi syndrome was normal. Electroretinogram is reduced. The phenotype is syndromic and ciliopathy-like.

A 12-year-old boy has recurrent episodes of fever, severe abdominal pain, and pleuritic chest pain lasting one to three days. Between attacks he feels well and attends school normally. Several emergency visits were attributed to viral gastroenteritis, but inflammatory markers rise during episodes. Examination during one episode shows erysipelas-like erythema over the ankle and mild arthritis. There is no chronic diarrhea, no immunodeficiency, and no evidence of appendicitis. Urinalysis shows intermittent proteinuria. Family ancestry is Armenian. The episodic serositis pattern has become more frequent.

A 9-year-old boy is referred for progressive leg stiffness and declining school performance. He walked normally until age five, then developed toe walking, frequent falls, and difficulty keeping up with peers. Examination shows lower-limb spasticity, paraparesis, brisk reflexes, and mild distal sensory loss. Brain MRI shows thinning and hypoplasia of the corpus callosum. There are no seizures, optic atrophy, or cardiomyopathy. A prior evaluation incorrectly focused on cerebral palsy, but symptoms are progressive. Family history includes consanguinity.

A 7-month-old boy is admitted for poor feeding and hypotonia after a winter respiratory infection. He also has eczema, reflux, and a family history of food allergies, which initially distracted from the progressive weakness. Over two months, parents noticed fewer leg movements and increasing fatigue during feeds. Echocardiogram now shows hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, while CK is elevated. There are no seizures, no tongue fasciculations, and no organomegaly. A neuromuscular panel includes variants in GAA, LMNA, and DES, but only one fits the enzyme deficiency. The respiratory illness appears to have unmasked an underlying progressive disorder.
true_disease: Glycogen storage disease due to acid maltase deficiency

clinical_note: A 17-year-old girl presents with chest discomfort after a minor sports injury, chronic fatigue, and worsening nearsightedness. She is tall and slender with pectus excavatum and scoliosis, but also has joint pain that led to an earlier suspicion of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Ophthalmology confirms ectopia lentis, and echocardiogram shows aortic root dilation. She denies easy skin tearing, recurrent dislocations, or history of arterial rupture. Her gene panel lists FBN1, TGFBR2, COL3A1, and COL5A1 as candidates. There are no inflammatory markers or autoimmune symptoms. The cardiovascular and ocular findings are the most specific features.

A 2-year-old boy with chronic ear infections and mild asthma is evaluated for developmental delay and progressive stiffness. He has coarse facial features, macroglossia, hepatosplenomegaly, and a history of umbilical hernia repair. Because he also has bruising and bone pain, Gaucher disease was considered, and a panel included IDUA, GBA, SMPD1, and IDS. Ophthalmology notes corneal clouding, and skeletal survey shows dysostosis multiplex. There are no episodes of acute neurologic regression or cherry-red spot. Hearing impairment is present, and sleep is noisy. The multisystem findings have steadily worsened since infancy.

A 5-year-old boy is referred for fractures, hearing concerns, and joint pain after several low-impact injuries. He also has mild skin hyperextensibility, which led one clinician to suspect a connective tissue disorder such as classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Examination shows blue sclerae, dentin abnormalities, osteopenia, and mild short stature. He has no aortic root dilation, no lens dislocation, and no severe easy bruising. Gene testing lists COL1A1, COL5A1, TNXB, and FBN1. Radiographs show multiple healed fractures at different stages. The skeletal fragility is the dominant feature.

A 3-week-old infant is readmitted for vomiting, poor feeding, and dehydration after initial discharge with a diagnosis of reflux. The chart also notes neonatal jaundice and transient hypoglycemia, but current labs show hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Examination shows ambiguous genitalia and diffuse hyperpigmentation. There is no fever, no structural bowel obstruction, and cultures remain negative. A steroidogenesis panel includes CYP21A2, HSD3B2, NR5A1, and STAR. The electrolyte pattern improves rapidly with glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid treatment. The presentation is noisy but strongly adrenal.

A 6-year-old boy with obesity and attention difficulties is evaluated for progressive weakness. His parents first attributed falls to weight gain, but he now struggles to climb stairs and uses his hands to rise from the floor. Examination shows calf hypertrophy, waddling gait, and proximal muscle weakness. CK is markedly elevated, and cardiac screening shows early cardiomyopathy. There is no sensory neuropathy, no ataxia, and no inflammatory myopathy rash. A neuromuscular panel includes DMD, FKRP, LMNA, and GAA. The distractor symptoms are chronic, but the motor decline is progressive and muscular.

A 39-year-old man is evaluated after several years of insomnia, depression, and new involuntary movements. His alcohol use and job stress initially made the psychiatric history seem primary. On exam he has chorea, impaired eye movements, and a wide-based gait. He denies antipsychotic exposure, and brain MRI shows caudate atrophy rather than stroke. Family history is unclear because he was adopted, and a broad neurologic panel includes HTT, PRNP, ATXN3, and SLC2A3. There are no seizures or copper metabolism abnormalities. The progressive behavioral and motor syndrome remains the key signal.

A 5-year-old boy is referred for cafe-au-lait macules, headaches, and intermittent blurry vision. Because his mother has schwannomas, the initial referral questioned NF2, and a tumor panel lists NF1, NF2, SPRED1, and TSC2. Examination shows axillary freckling and multiple soft subcutaneous nodules, while ophthalmology identifies Lisch nodules. MRI shows a small optic pathway glioma but no bilateral vestibular schwannomas. He has mild learning difficulty and attention problems. There are no hypomelanotic macules, seizures, or cortical tubers. The skin and optic findings point to the correct neurocutaneous syndrome.
